source.title: The good, the bad and the ugly sides of data augmentation: An implicit spectral regularization perspective
source.authors: Chi-Heng Lin; Chiraag Kaushik; Eva L. Dyer; Vidya K. Muthukumar

record.tranche_reason: The study empirically examines test-error curves around interpolation in linear regression, including the effect of training-sample count. This bears conceptually on sample-wise double descent, but it does not reproduce the original deep-network size or epoch sweeps.
record.gate_note: The relevant results are the study's own sample-size sweeps and error decompositions in Section 6.4 and Figure 7. Other mentions of double descent cite prior work and are not recorded as results. The text describes peak positions and trends, but supplies no numerical test-error values for Figure 7.
record.test_reason: Section 6.4 reports the study's own sample-count sweeps and error decompositions in linear regression, testing sample-wise double descent and its dependence on augmentation and variance.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate with one qualification: smaller finite pre-computed augmentations retain and shift the peak to n ≈ p/k, but it almost disappears for k > 8. aERM error decreases monotonically. The authors connect suppression to variance reduction and propose, without proving, that finite-augmentation randomness explains the additional bias peak.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses synthetic linear regression and compares pre-computed data augmentations with aERM, rather than sweeping deep-network size or training epochs as in the cited double-descent work.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported curve differs between pre-computed augmentation and aERM. For pre-computed augmentation, peak location depends on augmentation size k; peak magnitude and width decrease as k grows. The study shows Gaussian-noise and random-mask comparisons.
record.problems: The double-descent evidence is from synthetic linear regression rather than deep networks. Figure 7 does not provide numerical test-error values or stated uncertainty for the reported curves. The sample-size sweep does not test model size or training epochs.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant results were left out. Figure 7 curve values are not transcribed as numbers because the text gives no numerical test-MSE values.

untested.parts: No test-error trajectory testing epoch-wise double descent; optimization-convergence experiments do not establish that shape.
No capacity sweep demonstrating a second descent beyond interpolation; sample count varies at fixed dimension.
No single effective-complexity measure predicts peak locations across size, epochs and samples. The n ≈ p/k observation concerns only augmented sample count.
Observation-noise strength is fixed in the relevant sweeps. Multiple peaks and disappearance under optimally tuned regularization are not tested.
No replotting against effective parameter count showing conversion to an ordinary U-shaped curve.

record.verdict_notes: The supplied text includes Figure 7 captions but no readable plotted values. Qualitative findings are explicitly stated in Sections 6.4 and 7.3. Section 7.3 says the threshold shifts right, contradicting Section 6.4, the caption and n ≈ p/k; the consistent direction is left. No verdict relies on that conflicting phrase.

versions.untested_parts: No sweep of deep-network model size.
No test-error sweep over training epochs.
The evidence is for synthetic linear regression, not the original deep-network settings; no numerical curve values are stated.
The study varies training-sample count, not model capacity across model classes.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as predicting peak location across axes.
The study reports bias and variance peak behavior, but does not vary label noise to identify its effect, test multiple or triple peaks, or test optimally tuned regularization.
No comparison of the curve against an effective parameter count.

rows.subject: pre-computing method
rows.operation_detail: Sweep training-sample count for estimators trained on pre-computed Gaussian-noise augmentations.
rows.measure: Test MSE as a function of training-sample count
rows.value: A double-descent peak is reported; for augmentation size k, its location is approximately n = 128/k.
rows.note: The text also says the peak's magnitude and width decrease as augmentation size grows, and it almost disappears when k > 8.
rows.check: Split by augmentation size: smaller finite k retains a peak near n = 128/k, whereas its magnitude and width shrink and it almost disappears for k > 8. One observed state cannot represent all k.

rows.note: This is a setting in which the sample-wise peak is not reported.
rows.check: Also bears on V6 through augmentation-induced regularization and peak suppression. Absent describes the interpolation peak; optimal regularization was not tested.
